idiom_name: goroutine worker pool over a jobs channel (fan-out/fan-in)
implementation_notes: Go has no future or pool type, and the local idiom replaces the master/slave object structure: the master sends work items on a jobs channel, N worker goroutines range over it and send partial results on a results channel, and a fan-in goroutine closes the results channel only after every send is done (sync.WaitGroup). sync.WaitGroup is the join and golang.org/x/sync/errgroup adds the error and cancellation policy plus SetLimit for a bounded concurrency without a hand-written pool; buffered channels or a semaphore provide back-pressure. The classic structure is justified when the pool must outlive the call, when per-worker state (a connection, a cache) must be reused, or when the dispatch order must be controlled.
code_sketch:
jobs := make(chan Part)
results := make(chan int64)
var wg sync.WaitGroup
for range runtime.NumCPU() {
    wg.Add(1)
    go func() { defer wg.Done(); for p := range jobs { results <- partialSum(p) } }()
}
go func() { for _, p := range parts { jobs <- p }; close(jobs); wg.Wait(); close(results) }()
var total int64
for r := range results { total += r }   // master aggregates
pitfalls: Goroutines are not garbage collected: a worker blocked sending on results leaks when the master stops receiving, so the fan-in close must happen only after all sends finish.
Result order is nondeterministic; aggregate commutatively or carry the subtask index instead of assuming submission order.
An unbounded goroutine-per-task pool is just goroutine-per-task: bound the concurrency with errgroup.SetLimit, a semaphore channel, or a fixed worker count.
